blocks.text: What the prophet Amos has about locusts.

To the objection raised above, that no one else mentions the locusts of Joel, Theodoret answers differently: namely, that besides Joel the prophet Amos also mentions καὶ ἀκρίδος, καὶ βρούχου, καὶ πυρώσεως, καὶ ἰκτέρου, καὶ συκῶν, καὶ ἐλαιῶν, καὶ ἀμπέλων, ὑπὸ καμπῶν διαφθειρομένων, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις αὐχμοῦ, καὶ ἀνομβρίας [kai akridos, kai brouchou, kai pyrōseōs, kai ikterou, kai sykōn, kai elaiōn, kai ampelōn, hypo kampōn diaphtheiromenōn, kai pros toutois auchmou, kai anombrias], both the locust and the bruchus, and burning and jaundice, and also the figs, olives and vines consumed by caterpillars, and moreover drought and lack of rain. He is evidently alluding to two passages. The first is Amos IV, 7. 8. 9. I withheld the rain from you when there were yet three months (remaining) to the harvest. And I sent rain upon one city, but upon another city I did not send rain. One part was rained upon, and the part on which it did not rain withered. And two or three cities wandered to one city to drink water, and were not satisfied, etc. I struck you with mildew and blight (in Greek ἐν πυρώσει, καὶ ἐν ἰκτέρῳ [en pyrōsei, kai en ikterō], with burning and jaundice). The multitude of your gardens and of your vineyards, and your figs and your olives, the הגזם gazam devoured (that is, the locust that attacks trees, not κάμπη [kampē], the caterpillar, as in the Greek and the Vulgate), yet you have not returned to me, says the Lord. The second is Amos VII, 1. 2. 3. Thus the Lord God showed me. He was forming גובי (gobai) locusts when the הלקש, the aftermath hay, first began to grow. And the aftermath hay was after the king's mowings. And it came to pass, when they had finished eating the grass of the land, that I said: Lord God, forgive, I beseech you. How shall Jacob stand? For he is small. The Lord (therefore) repented of this. It shall not be, says the Lord. Theodoret, comparing these two passages with Joel, thought that both prophets described the same calamity, the one as future, the other as past. But how truly, I do not quite know, since Joel and Amos differ not a little in many respects. In the former there is extreme drought everywhere.

— — — fiery thirst drains the fields, the waters have fled, springs and lakes lie parched, and hollow rivers harden with seething mud, [III, 321] a sickly leanness is on the soil, and the crop droops from the very base of the tender stalk; the herd stands cheated at the margin of the bank, and the cattle seek the rivers they once swam ^{a)}.

See Joel, chapter 1, verses 18. 19. 20. But in chapter 4 of Amos God sends rain in one place and not in another, and while one part is rained upon, the other withers. There the gazam alone appears; in Joel, besides the gazam, three other kinds of locusts lay waste Judaea [col. 484], and they not only consume the produce of the trees, as in Amos, but also damage and wither the trees themselves, Ioel. I, 12. And the peoples whom Amos reproaches for impenitence turn to God in Joel, and implore his mercy with fasting and prayers. Again, in chapter 7 of Amos God does not form the locusts until after the mowings, when the aftermath hay had already grown up. So, the harvest being already completed, they harm only the grass. But in Joel the wheat and barley are laid waste, and the harvest of the field perishes. Finally Amos, interceding alone for Israel, at once averts the approaching evil. But in Joel the priests, and from among the people the old men, the young men, even the children still hanging at the breast, are summoned to the house of God by the blast of the trumpet, to entreat God with common supplications. Nor is he easily moved, but only after this evil had continued for several years. It is therefore hardly probable that Amos narrates as fulfilled the very things that Joel had foretold, since they disagree in so many points.
